prompt: Let $P,Q,R$ be classical propositions; $\top$ means true, $\bot$ means false, and $\equiv$ means equal truth values under every assignment. Which proposed identity fails for some truth assignment, showing that the commutative law cannot be used for every binary connective?

answers.explanation: Take the first proposition true and the second false. The forward implication is false, but the reversed implication is true. Swapping antecedent and consequent is therefore not a valid equivalence.
Conjunction is true exactly when both inputs are true, regardless of their order. This identity holds for every assignment.
Inclusive disjunction is true exactly when at least one input is true, regardless of order. This identity always holds.
A biconditional tests equality of the input truth values. Equality is unaffected by swapping them, so this identity always holds.
Both sides require all three inputs to be true. This associative law always holds.
Both sides require at least one of the three inputs to be true. This associative law always holds.
Both sides are false exactly when the antecedent is true and the consequent false. This identity always holds.
Reversing the direction and negating both inputs gives contraposition, which is valid. It does not justify reversing the direction alone.
Both sides are false exactly when the antecedent is true and both possible consequents are false. The identity holds for every assignment.
Only the conjunction inside the antecedent is reordered. Its truth value is unchanged, so the complete implication is unchanged too.
